samf-senior-2016-r2-02.title: Prime factorisation
samf-senior-2016-r2-02.body:
$2016=2^5\cdot3^2\cdot7$. A perfect square needs every exponent even, so $x$ must contain one more $2$ and one $7$. The smallest is $x=2\cdot7=14$, giving $2016\cdot14=168^2$.

**Answer: 14**

samf-senior-2016-r2-03.title: AM-GM
samf-senior-2016-r2-03.body:
For positive numbers, $\dfrac ab+\dfrac ba\ge2\sqrt{\dfrac ab\cdot\dfrac ba}=2$, with equality for $a=b$.

**Answer: 2**

samf-senior-2016-r2-04.title: Find the big square
samf-senior-2016-r2-04.body:
The shaded squares have sides $3,4,5,7$. The two larger squares (sides $7$ and $5$) are side by side along one side of the big square, so its side is $7+5=12$ and its area is $144$. The unshaded area is $144-(9+16+25+49)=144-99=45$.

**Answer: 45**

samf-senior-2016-r2-05.title: Triangle inequality
samf-senior-2016-r2-05.body:
The third side must be less than $5+7=12$. The largest prime below $12$ is $11$, and $5,7,11$ does form a triangle ($5+7>11$ and $11<5+7$, $7<5+11$).

**Answer: 11**

samf-senior-2016-r2-06.title: Interpolate
samf-senior-2016-r2-06.body:
$80^\circ$C is $80\%$ of the way from freezing to boiling. On the SAMO scale the range is $170-20=150$, so the reading is $20+0.8\times150=140$.

**Answer: 140**

samf-senior-2016-r2-07.title: Euler trail argument
samf-senior-2016-r2-07.body:
The network has $6$ junctions; every junction (corners and edge midpoints) is met by an even number of paths ($2$ or $4$). A walk from $X$ to $Y$ that uses a set of paths needs $X$ and $Y$ to meet an odd number of used paths and every other junction an even number. $X$ and $Y$ each meet only $2$ paths, so a walk from $X$ to $Y$ uses exactly one of them at each end; the unused paths therefore meet $X$ and $Y$ an odd number of times and every other junction an even number of times, which forces at least a connection from $X$ to $Y$: at least two unused paths (the two along the side $XY$ work). The remaining seven paths can be walked from $X$ to $Y$. The maximum is $7\times100=700$ m.

**Answer: 700**

samf-senior-2016-r2-08.title: Sum is 11 times digit sum
samf-senior-2016-r2-08.body:
If $N=10x+y$ then $N+\text{reverse}=11(x+y)$. This is a perfect square only if $11\mid(x+y)$ with $11(x+y)$ square, i.e. $x+y=11$ (as $1\le x+y\le18$), giving $121$. The pairs are $(2,9),(3,8),(4,7),(5,6),(6,5),(7,4),(8,3),(9,2)$: $29,38,47,56,65,74,83,92$, so $8$ numbers.

**Answer: 8**

samf-senior-2016-r2-09.title: Follow the touching faces
samf-senior-2016-r2-09.body:
Opposite faces add to $9$ and touching faces add to $10$. The cube whose outer face shows $3$ has $6$ on its opposite (touching) face, so the face it touches is $4$, whose opposite face is $5$; that touches a $5$, and so on along the chain. The last touching pair is $7$ and $3$, so the face carrying $*$ is opposite a $3$ and $*=9-3=6$.

**Answer: 6**

samf-senior-2016-r2-10.title: Divisibility
samf-senior-2016-r2-10.body:
Among three consecutive odd integers exactly one is a multiple of $3$ (their differences are $2$ and $4$, so they cover all residues mod $3$), so $3\mid P$ always. Also $1\cdot3\cdot5=15$ and $7\cdot9\cdot11=693=3\cdot 231$ have $\gcd(15,693)=3$. So the highest common factor is $3$.

**Answer: 3**

samf-senior-2016-r2-11.title: Inscribed angle
samf-senior-2016-r2-11.body:
Let $O$ be the centre. Then $OA=OB=AB$, so $\triangle OAB$ is equilateral and $\angle AOB=60^\circ$. The inscribed angle on the same chord, $\angle ACB$, is half the central angle: $30^\circ$.

**Answer: 30**

samf-senior-2016-r2-13.title: Balance the sweets
samf-senior-2016-r2-13.body:
Let tails appear $t$ times, so heads appear $30-t$ times. Simon receives $3t$ sweets and gives $2(30-t)$. These are equal: $3t=60-2t$, so $t=12$.

**Answer: 12**

samf-senior-2016-r2-14.title: Remove the largest numbers
samf-senior-2016-r2-14.body:
The first $50$ even integers sum to $2+4+\cdots+100=50\cdot51=2550$. We must remove numbers with sum $2550-2016=534$. The five largest, $100+98+96+94+92=480<534$, so five numbers are not enough, but six are: remove $100,98,96,94,92$ and $54$ (sum $534$). The minimum is $6$.

**Answer: 6**

samf-senior-2016-r2-15.title: Pythagoras in 3D
samf-senior-2016-r2-15.body:
In the plane, $BC^2=BD^2+CD^2=1+3=4$. Since $AB$ is perpendicular to the plane, $AD^2=AB^2+BD^2=3+1=4$ and $AC^2=AB^2+BC^2=3+4=7$. Then $AD^2+DC^2=4+3=7=AC^2$, so by the converse of Pythagoras $\angle ADC=90^\circ$.

**Answer: 90**

samf-senior-2016-r2-16.title: Ratios of areas on a line
samf-senior-2016-r2-16.body:
Triangles with the same apex and bases on line $DC$ have areas in the ratio of their bases. From apex $A$: $DE:EC=6:10$, so $DE=\frac{3}{8}DC$. From apex $B$: $DF:FC=17:7$, so $DF=\frac{17}{24}DC$. Then $EF=DF-DE=\frac{17-9}{24}DC=\frac13DC$. Triangle $BDC$ has area $17+7=24$, so $[BEF]=\frac13\cdot24=8$.

**Answer: 8**

samf-senior-2016-r2-17.title: Subtract the equations
samf-senior-2016-r2-17.body:
Clearing fractions: $c^2x+2a^2y=2a^2c^2$ and $2b^2x+c^2y=2b^2c^2$. Subtract: $(c^2-2b^2)x+(2a^2-c^2)y=2c^2(a^2-b^2)$. By Pythagoras $c^2=a^2+b^2$, so $c^2-2b^2=2a^2-c^2=a^2-b^2\ne0$. Dividing by $a^2-b^2$: $x+y=2c^2=18$.

**Answer: 18**

samf-senior-2016-r2-20.title: Incircle and excircles
samf-senior-2016-r2-20.body:
Let the triangle have right angle at $B$, legs $AB=p$, $BC=q$, hypotenuse $AC=h$ and semi-perimeter $s$. The circle $D$ is the incircle; $E$ and $F$ are the excircles opposite $A$ and $C$; $G$ is the excircle opposite $B$. Use the fact that the tangent length from a vertex to the excircle opposite that vertex is $s$.

- Excircle $G$: its centre is equidistant from the lines $BA$ and $BC$, which are perpendicular, so its radius equals the tangent length from $B$: $\rho_G=s$.
- Excircle opposite $A$: the radius equals the tangent length from $B$, and the tangent length from $A$ is $p+\rho$, which equals $s$. So $\rho=s-p$. Likewise the excircle opposite $C$ has radius $s-q$.
- Incircle: tangent lengths from $B$ are $r$, so $(p-r)+(q-r)=h$ and $r=s-h$.

Hence $r+\rho_A+\rho_C=(s-h)+(s-p)+(s-q)=3s-2s=s=\rho_G$. So $\rho_G=3+4+21=28$.

**Answer: 28**

samf-senior-2016-r2-20.title: Product relation
samf-senior-2016-r2-20.body:
For a right triangle, $r\cdot\rho_G=(s-h)s=\text{area}$ (since $rs=$ area) and $\rho_A\rho_C=(s-p)(s-q)=\frac{h^2-(p-q)^2}{4}=\frac{pq}{2}=$ area. So $r\rho_G=\rho_A\rho_C$, i.e. $3\rho_G=4\cdot21$ and $\rho_G=28$.

**Answer: 28**
